opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me, it's great to be back.

I think about it in terms of a spectrum. At one end is what I'd call incremental, "normal science": you have a well-defined problem, a clear evaluation metric, and you search a space of hypotheses or code changes to push the number up. AI systems are already genuinely useful there. With LLM-driven search, especially combined with evolutionary approaches where you keep a population of candidate solutions, mutate them, and select on fitness, you can discover algorithms, loss functions, or optimizers that humans hadn't tried. That's real, and it's scaling quickly.

At the other end are the paradigm shifts, the things that change what questions we ask in the first place. I'm more cautious there. A lot of what makes a discovery "major" isn't solving a hard problem; it's recognizing that a problem is interesting, or reframing an anomaly everyone else ignored. That requires open-endedness: generating new goals, not just optimizing fixed ones. Current systems are still largely bound by the objectives and evaluators we hand them, and they inherit the priors of their training data, so they tend to stay close to what's already known.

That's why I find open-endedness research so important. If you look at how science actually progresses, it's a collective, cumulative process, an archive of stepping stones where something useless today becomes the key to something else ten years later. If we want AI to contribute major innovations, we need systems that build up and explore that kind of archive, with good measures of novelty and interestingness, not just correctness.

There's also the verification problem. In domains with cheap, reliable feedback, like code, math with formal proofs, or simulations, AI can iterate thousands of times and you can trust the result. In wet-lab biology or anything that needs expensive real-world experiments, the bottleneck shifts from generating ideas to testing them. So I expect the first big AI-driven breakthroughs to come where evaluation is automatable, and then spread as we connect these systems to automated labs.

So my honest answer: AI is already a powerful engine for discovery within a frame, and I'm optimistic it can become a genuine collaborator in reframing too. But that won't come from scaling alone. It'll come from designing systems that can decide for themselves what's worth pursuing, and from keeping humans in the loop to judge which of those directions actually matter.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the honest answer is that I'm quite bullish, but maybe for slightly different reasons than people expect. When people ask "can AI do science," they often have this picture of a single eureka moment, the Einstein-in-the-patent-office kind of thing, and they ask whether a language model can have that. And I actually think that's the wrong frame for where the leverage is right now.

If you look at how science is actually practiced, especially in machine learning, a huge fraction of the work is not the single brilliant idea. It's reading the literature, forming a hypothesis, writing the code, running the experiment, realizing the experiment was broken, fixing it, running it again, writing it up, and then having it torn apart in review. That whole loop is slow, expensive, and a lot of it is honestly quite mechanical. And what we've found, with the AI Scientist work and then with the follow-ups, is that you can automate that entire loop end to end. Not perfectly, but genuinely end to end: idea generation, experimentation, writing a paper, and even an automated review step.

Now, the key question is: is what comes out of that pipeline actually novel? And I'd be careful here. A lot of what these systems produce today is what I'd call incremental, well, "normal science" in the Kuhnian sense. Combining two existing ideas, applying a known method to a new setting, running an ablation nobody bothered to run. And I think people underrate how much of real scientific progress is exactly that. Most human papers are also that. So even if the system is "only" doing normal science, if it can do it at a thousand times the throughput and a tiny fraction of the cost, that changes the dynamics of a field.

Where I'm more uncertain is on the paradigm-shift side. The really big innovations usually come from someone having a weird prior, being stubborn about it, and being willing to go against the consensus of the field for years. Current models are trained on the consensus. They're very good at interpolating within the distribution of what's been published, and they're less naturally inclined to make the contrarian bet. So one of the things I think about a lot is: how do you build systems that explore more aggressively, that generate diverse hypotheses rather than the mode of the distribution? That's actually where my background in evolutionary methods and open-endedness comes in. You want search processes that reward novelty and surprise, not just agreement with what's already known.

And then there's the verification side, which I think is the thing that actually makes this work. The reason you can let a system run thousands of experiments is that in ML, and in computational science more broadly, you have a ground truth you can check. The code runs or it doesn't, the metric goes up or it doesn't. The model can be wrong in its reasoning a hundred times, and as long as the experimental feedback is real, you can still make progress. That's very different from asking a model to just reason its way to a discovery in its head.

So if you ask me where we are, I'd say: we're already at the point where AI can produce the long tail of scientific contributions, the stuff that fills in the map. And I think over the next few years the interesting question becomes whether, at sufficient scale and with the right exploration pressure, the paradigm shifts emerge out of that volume, or whether that requires something qualitatively different that we haven't built yet. I lean toward the former, but I hold that view fairly loosely.

astra-6.text:
I think the exciting possibility is that AI can help us search over ideas and experiments at a scale that we simply couldn’t manage ourselves. But there’s a distinction between generating something that looks like an interesting scientific idea and actually making a discovery. You need a way to test it, learn from the result, and decide what to try next.

That makes me particularly interested in domains where you can close that loop—where a system can propose an algorithm, run it, and get meaningful feedback. You could imagine it finding solutions that a human wouldn’t naturally consider, because it doesn’t have exactly the same intuitions or biases. Of course, it will have its own biases, coming from the training data and the way we define success.

The harder question is whether it can change the questions we ask. Optimizing against an existing benchmark is one thing; realizing that we’re measuring the wrong thing, or finding a new way to frame a problem, is another. I don’t see a fundamental reason why AI couldn’t contribute there, but I’m uncertain about how reliably we can get that behavior. For me, the most compelling prospect is a feedback loop between people, AI systems, and experiments, where each helps expose what the others are missing.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the interesting distinction is between generating a new idea and knowing that it’s a good idea. We’re getting very good at building systems that can propose candidates—hypotheses, algorithms, experiments. But a scientific breakthrough also requires a way to test those candidates and learn from the results.

So I’m particularly excited about domains where you can close that loop: propose something, run a simulation or an experiment, get feedback, and improve the next proposal. If the feedback is reliable, you can search for things that a human researcher might never think to try.

The harder question is whether the system can change the problem formulation itself. Can it recognize that we’re asking the wrong question, or that we need a different representation? I don’t think we should assume that simply scaling up the production of plausible ideas automatically gets us there.

But I also wouldn’t make human-style understanding a prerequisite. A system could produce a genuinely important discovery through a process that looks very different from how we do science. What matters is whether the result survives testing and gives us something useful to build on.
